\begin{keybox}[title=Headline result]
\small
On a \nAuthors{}-author closed set of public-domain Bangla prose
(\nPassages{} passages, \nWorks{} works, \nTokens{} tokens), the best
attributor reaches \textbf{\bestAcc{}} accuracy against \chanceAcc{} chance
--- on a \textbf{work-disjoint} split, where no book has passages on both
sides.  The same pipeline scores \randomSplitAcc{} on a naive random split;
that \leakGap{} gap is topic leakage, not style.
\end{keybox}

\end{titlepage}

% ------------------------------------------------------------------ abstract
\begin{abstract}
\noindent
We build a multi-author Bangla stylometric pipeline over public-domain prose
from Bengali Wikisource and use it to compare a \emph{generative} attribution
paradigm --- one Kneser--Ney language model per author, attribute to the lowest
perplexity --- against a \emph{discriminative} one --- a linear SVM over
stylometric and embedding features, and a fine-tuned BanglaBERT.  Alongside
this we ask a representation-level question: in a small-corpus regime, do
pretrained embeddings or embeddings trained from scratch on the author corpus
better isolate style from topic?

The corpus is \nPassages{} passages drawn from \nWorks{} works by \nAuthors{}
authors spanning 1820--1951, filtered to Wikisource pages the community has
marked proofread.  Because no usable Bangla POS tagger was available in this
environment, one was written and validated at \posAcc{} token accuracy against
the Universal Dependencies Bengali treebank.

Our central methodological finding is that \textbf{splitting by passage rather
than by work inflates accuracy by \leakGap{}} --- \randomSplitAcc{} against
\workSplitAcc{} for the identical model.  Every result we report is from the
work-disjoint split, and we argue that published Bangla attribution figures
should state which regime they used.
\end{abstract}
